title: French Students Protest Nationwide as Hundreds of Schools Shut Down – Al Jazeera Report
body:
The wave of student‑led demonstrations that began in early September has entered its third week, and the unrest shows no sign of abating. Across France, hundreds of schools have shut their doors as pupils, teachers and parents rally against chronic teacher shortages, deteriorating school conditions and what they describe as a government that has failed to safeguard the future of public education. The protests turned deadly in the northern city of Lens on Monday, where a 15‑year‑old student lost a hand after a grenade‑type explosive detonated during a clash with police, prompting a formal investigation by the national police oversight body.

The protests, initially sparked by a series of strikes organized by the national teachers’ union (SNP), have broadened into a wider social movement that now includes secondary‑school students and university undergraduates. Demonstrators have staged sit‑ins inside classrooms, blocked school entrances and organized mass walk‑outs, demanding immediate recruitment drives, better pay for teachers and urgent upgrades to school infrastructure. In Paris, more than 1,200 pupils gathered in front of the Ministry of Education, waving banners that read “Our future is not a bargaining chip.” Similar scenes unfolded in Lyon, Marseille and Lille, where local authorities reported that over 70 per cent of secondary schools were either partially or fully closed due to safety concerns or staff shortages.

The Lens incident has intensified the political stakes of the unrest. According to preliminary reports, the teenager was among a group of students who attempted to breach a police cordon surrounding a school that had been occupied by protesters. Police deployed tear‑gas canisters and a hand‑held grenade‑type device, which exploded prematurely, causing the severe injury. The French General Inspectorate of the National Police (IGPN) has launched an inquiry into the use of the explosive, and the Ministry of the Interior has pledged a transparent review of police tactics. Opposition parties have seized on the episode, accusing the government of excessive force, while the ruling coalition argues that law‑enforcement actions were necessary to prevent a larger escalation.

The underlying grievances fueling the protests are rooted in a decade‑long decline in education funding and a series of reforms that have strained the system. France’s public school workforce has shrunk by roughly 7 per cent since 2015, leaving many classrooms without a permanent teacher and prompting an over‑reliance on temporary contracts. In rural departments, some schools operate with a single educator responsible for multiple grades, a situation that has prompted parents to withdraw their children and enroll them in private institutions, further widening educational inequality. Moreover, aging school buildings, inadequate heating and insufficient digital resources have become flashpoints for students who feel their learning environment is being neglected.

The government’s response has been a mixture of concession and firmness. Education Minister Pap Ndiaye announced a €3.5 billion emergency fund aimed at recruiting 4,000 new teachers over the next two years and earmarked resources for renovating 150 schools deemed “critical.” Simultaneously, the interior ministry has reinforced police presence around protest sites and issued new directives authorizing the use of “non‑lethal” crowd‑control equipment in “dangerous” scenarios. Critics argue that the financial package, while sizable, is insufficient to reverse years of disinvestment and that the security clampdown risks further alienating a generation already distrustful of state institutions.

As the protests continue into the second half of October, the trajectory of France’s education debate will likely hinge on the outcome of the IGPN investigation and the government’s ability to translate announced funding into tangible improvements on the ground. If the authorities can demonstrate swift recruitment, concrete upgrades to school facilities, and a calibrated approach to policing, they may defuse the most volatile flashpoints. Conversely, prolonged school closures and a perception of heavy‑handed law enforcement could deepen societal divides and embolden broader labor unrest. All eyes remain on Paris, where upcoming parliamentary sessions are expected to debate a comprehensive education reform bill that could reshape the nation’s schooling system for years to come.
